question: How many apparently new themes can you trace back to the opening’s few gestures?
intro: Liszt makes a single continuous sonata out of a few sharply differentiated ideas, transforming them into song, declamation and fugue. Jorge Bolet’s 1960 recording gives the whole design, including the quiet ending after its largest late climax.

cues.title: Notes separated by silence
cues.text: The slow introduction places separated notes around descending scales. Store the scale’s shape as well as the spaces between attacks: its return near the end will help connect the closing music to this hesitant beginning.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies m. 1 opening material. Analysis shows very low levels through 0:30 before the first major increase.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two forceful gestures
cues.text: The opening Allegro introduces a leaping octave-and-triplet idea and a hammered repeated-note figure. They sound unlike the slow scales, but all three become building material rather than disposable introductions.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies motifs at mm. 8 and 13. Analysis shows the abrupt level increase near 0:35; individual bars are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remember rhythm as well
cues.text: Try remembering the attack pattern of each gesture rather than a complete melody. Liszt can change register, key and articulation so extensively that rhythm becomes the quickest clue to a familiar idea.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt based on the thematic-transformation account in https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One movement several perspectives
cues.text: The Sonata can be followed both as a large sonata-form argument and as a continuous sequence containing slow-movement and scherzo-like regions. Those readings overlap; no pause announces four separate conventional movements.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ discusses the double-function design and competing placements of its recapitulation.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A broader kind of statement
cues.text: The score’s Grandioso idea offers broad chordal declamation against the opening’s broken, driven gestures. In this region, listen for the change of scale: a larger melodic span can still belong to the same continuous argument.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ locates Grandioso at m. 105. Analysis boundary 2:24 and D-major region around 2:55–3:05 support approximate placement, not a bar attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The weight begins to lift
cues.text: The broad span gives way to a markedly quieter stretch. Carry the opening’s gestures into that change: a lyrical surface need not mean that Liszt has discarded his earlier material.
cues.evidence: Analysis falls to −26.2 dB at 3:30, −31.5 at 3:35 and −40.1 at 3:45; boundary 3:28.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Weimar rather than the tour
cues.text: Liszt completes the Sonata in 1853 during his Weimar years, after withdrawing from the career of a travelling virtuoso. Its concentration on transforming a small store of ideas belongs to that period of sustained composition.
cues.evidence: Liszt biography on the site; https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ gives completion in 1853.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A rough gesture becomes song
cues.text: One lyrical idea grows out of the earlier hammered repeated-note figure. The transformation changes the phrase’s character through sustained singing and altered accompaniment; a new manner does not necessarily require a new melodic source.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ compares the repeated-note motif with the cantando espressivo transformation at m. 153. This is a general relationship, not an entrance timed to 4:40.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Hear beneath the decoration
cues.text: In the quieter lyrical writing, follow the longer melody through the accompanying notes. Distinguishing tune from figuration makes it easier to recognise a transformed gesture when it later regains force.
cues.evidence: General prompt about the Sonata’s lyrical transformations; https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Transformation keeps the span moving
cues.text: The lyrical material does not settle into an isolated song movement. Listen for fragments of the earlier ideas to interrupt, extend or reshape it as the continuous development gathers momentum.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ describes the exposition’s transformed material and its subsequent development; passage-level formal account.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A renewed forceful turn
cues.text: The quieter middle of this span gives way to a strong rise in recorded level. Compare the attacks with the earlier Allegro: the contrast now carries the memory of the intervening lyrical transformation.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundary 6:58; −22.2 dB at 6:50 rises to −10.3 at 7:00 and −8.1 at 7:05.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Follow the bass direction
cues.text: Throughout the developing argument, keep a separate ear on the bass. Changing the foundation beneath a familiar melodic figure can make it sound unstable even when its rhythm remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt; thematic transformations and harmonic movement discussed in https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Force is sustained then renewed
cues.text: The stronger writing persists across several local rises. Distinguish a repeated attack from a real point of arrival: a loud chord can propel the phrase forward instead of ending it.
cues.evidence: Analysis remains strong near 8:00 and rises to −7.7 dB at 8:25 and −7.5 at 8:35; no chord function inferred from machine key labels.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A contrast inside the development
cues.text: The next reduction in force is substantial, but it does not yet begin the central Andante. Hear the intervening withdrawals and renewed attacks as part of the development’s unsettled scale.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −16.6 dB at 9:00 falls to −36.2 at 9:25; a fresh strong window follows at 9:30. The longer Andante begins later, near 11:00.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A dedication to Schumann
cues.text: The Sonata is dedicated to Robert Schumann. A dedication identifies an artistic relationship, not a hidden programme: the listener can follow the transformations without assigning the themes to fictional characters.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ documents the Schumann dedication and discusses the absence of an established composer-supplied programme.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Contrasts grow more extreme
cues.text: The approach to the central slow region alternates force with deep withdrawals. Listen through the gaps rather than counting them as movement endings; Liszt keeps the large work continuous.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −10.8 dB at 9:30, −34.8 at 9:45, renewed −12.4 at 10:25, then −41.1 by 10:55.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Prepare for a slower scale
cues.text: The long withdrawal makes room for a new pace of thought. Keep the earlier lyrical material in memory: the central slow region changes the span and harmonic setting rather than erasing everything heard so far.
cues.evidence: Analysis: quiet 10:45–10:55 precedes the sustained quieter F-sharp-major region around 11:00–11:15; score marks Andante sostenuto at m. 331.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The central Andante
cues.text: The Andante sostenuto gives F♯ major a central role and lets the line breathe on a wider scale. This is a slow region inside the continuous Sonata, not a separately numbered movement with a fresh start.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies m. 331 and F-sharp major. Audio chroma around 11:10–11:15 supports, but does not alone establish, this score-based location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hold the longer sentence
cues.text: Let the melody’s long direction matter more than each accompaniment note. The slower span changes the listener’s sense of proportion: a small melodic continuation can carry weight without a forceful attack.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt for the central Andante, identified from the score analysis and the quieter 11:00–12:30 span.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The slow span begins to grow
cues.text: The central region does not remain uniformly hushed. Its increase in level gives the sustained melodic line a larger reach without requiring a return to the opening’s sharply broken rhetoric.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −30.4 dB at 12:30 rises to −20 at 12:35 and −18.8 at 12:40.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Listen for connected singing
cues.text: Through the central rise, attend to how a melodic line continues across a change of register or chord spacing. The piano cannot sustain like a bowed instrument; the continuity depends on the shaping of successive attacks.
cues.evidence: General piano-listening prompt; it does not claim a particular fingering, pedal change or vocal imitation in Bolet’s performance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A climax within the slow region
cues.text: The Andante’s larger span reaches its own strong crest. Compare this with the opening’s impact: force now comes after a long lyrical expansion rather than after the introductory silence.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −9.6 dB at 13:45 and −7.6 at 14:10; score analysis places a central F-sharp-major climax at m. 397. Exact bar timing is not asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The crest withdraws
cues.text: The central climax gives way to a much quieter aftermath. Listen for the melodic remnants through the retreat; a reduction of force can preserve the argument while making its next direction uncertain.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −7.6 dB at 14:10 drops to −22.7 at 14:30 and −37.2 by 14:45.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Published without a story
cues.text: The Sonata appears in print in 1854. Later writers propose Faustian and other programmes, but Liszt supplies no authoritative narrative key for this score; its musical relationships remain the secure starting point.
cues.evidence: Yale University Library’s first-edition exhibit explicitly dates publication to 1854 and distinguishes later Faust readings from Liszt’s lack of a written programme: https://musiclib-exhibits.library.yale.edu/exhibits/liszt/bminor_sonata.html
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A long quiet aftermath
cues.text: The low-intensity passage extends far beyond a single breath between sections. Preserve the opening gestures in memory during this suspended span: their next transformation will depend on rhythm and contrapuntal combination.
cues.evidence: Analysis: low levels around 16:00, 16:30 and 16:50, with −46.3 dB at 16:50; no exact harmonic suspension is claimed.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Wait for a different texture
cues.text: Listen for the coming change from broad or isolated gestures to entries that answer one another. A fugato can make a familiar idea active in several voices rather than presenting a wholly new tune.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies the fugato at m. 460; the cue prepares for the region around 17:25 rather than claiming it has already begun.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The fugato approaches
cues.text: In the fugato, the earlier leaping and repeated-note ideas become contrapuntal material. The texture turns their identities into a game of entries and overlap, combining what the opening first separated.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ discusses m. 460, initially in B-flat minor. Analysis shows growing onset density and level from 17:20–17:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bülow gives the première
cues.text: Hans von Bülow gives the Sonata’s public première in Berlin in 1857. The work’s single-span design reaches listeners as a performed argument, not simply a catalogue of Liszt’s keyboard effects.
cues.evidence: The site’s Liszt biography, Weimar section, documents Bülow’s Berlin public première in 1857. https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html independently names Bülow’s first performance on 22 January 1857.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Imitation accumulates force
cues.text: The contrapuntal region grows denser and stronger as it moves towards the main return. Listen for the entries to cooperate in building momentum, rather than treating each one as an independent interruption.
cues.evidence: Analysis: higher onset density around 18:00, then −15.9 dB at 18:20 and −10.8 by 18:40. The formal source links the fugato to the return at m. 533.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B minor returns with history
cues.text: The principal return restores B minor and the opening’s forceful material, but the intervening slow region and fugato change its context. Recognition now includes several versions of each gesture, not only its first appearance.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies the B-minor recapitulation at m. 533. Audio supports a strong B-minor region around 18:55–19:10; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A return is not a reset
cues.text: Compare the returning material with what you remember from the beginning. Notice how altered continuations and destinations can make familiar music lead somewhere different instead of simply replaying the exposition.
cues.evidence: General recapitulation listening prompt supported by the formal account in https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: From force towards lyricism
cues.text: After another strong crest, the recorded level recedes again. The Sonata repeats its basic power to turn a forceful gesture into a singing one; try to recognise the shared shape across the change of character.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −7.8 dB at 20:20, then −20.9 at 20:35; lower levels follow into the later lyrical passage.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Let the softer line carry
cues.text: In this quieter span, focus on the melody’s contour rather than the number of notes around it. Earlier transformations make it possible to recognise an idea by direction and rhythm even when its weight has changed.
cues.evidence: Analysis: very quiet windows at 21:25–21:30; the text is a general listening strategy, not a specific theme entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A recording dated 1960
cues.text: The source identifies Jorge Bolet and the year 1960, but not a session venue or original issue number. Those missing details should not be supplied from another Bolet performance: this guide follows the selected file only.
cues.evidence: Commons description: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Liszt-_sonata_In_B_Minor_(piano_-_Jorge_Bolet_-_1960).mp3
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Gathering the late momentum
cues.text: The final large ascent grows out of the preceding quieter music. Keep the transformed themes in mind as the sound gains weight; the culmination belongs to their accumulated history, not merely to faster or louder playing.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −25.7 dB at 22:40 rises to −13.1 at 22:55 and −13 at 23:05.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The late culmination grows
cues.text: The recorded level rises through this late span towards the performance’s strongest window. The scale of the ascent suggests an emphatic conclusion, making the ensuing change of direction especially important.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −8.9 dB at 23:20, −8.1 at 23:35 and maximum −5.3 at 23:55.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Loudness does not decide the ending
cues.text: The strongest late writing is not the Sonata’s last word. Stay with the abrupt withdrawal that follows: the work still has its slow opening material to reconsider.
cues.evidence: Analysis: strong windows at 24:00 and 24:15, boundary at 24:16, then −32.6 dB at 24:20.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A quiet ending takes over
cues.text: After the late climax, the final Andante replaces public-sounding force with quiet recollection. The Sonata closes by revisiting its material on a smaller scale, rather than by sustaining the preceding triumphal weight.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ locates the final Andante at m. 711. Audio’s sharp withdrawal near 24:16 anchors the approximate boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remembered ideas change their order
cues.text: In the concluding pages, the opening’s principal gestures are recollected in reverse order. This is not a literal rewind: changing their register, pacing and harmonic setting gives familiar fragments a different function.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ identifies returns of the repeated-note, leaping and scale ideas at mm. 729, 737 and 750. No individual bar is aligned to 25:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Space becomes part of the phrase
cues.text: The ending allows more room around its quieter sounds. Recall how the introduction separated its notes: the physical space can resemble the beginning while the tonal destination gives it a different meaning.
cues.evidence: Analysis shows sustained low levels through 26:00–26:30. General comparison of the opening and closing textures, not a quantified tempo claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: B major rather than B minor
cues.text: The written ending settles in B major. Its quietness is essential to the design: tonal resolution and maximum volume are deliberately separated, after the late climax has already spent its force.
cues.evidence: https://www.classicalmusic-notes.com/liszt-sonata-1/ discusses the quiet B-major ending. This cue describes the final span, not an exact cadence at 26:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allow the last decay
cues.text: Stay with the final sound as it dies away. The recording’s last seconds complete the Sonata’s retreat from its late climax; they are not an invitation to supply a louder ending in the imagination.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −46.1 dB at 27:20, −51.8 at 27:25 and −66 dB at 27:30.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: Isolated scales give way to forceful gestures
transitions.how: The introductory scales and separated notes yield to leaping and repeated-note material with much sharper attack. The register and texture expand suddenly, but the introduction remains part of the thematic store that the Sonata will transform and eventually recall.
transitions.evidence: Score analysis mm. 1–13; abrupt level rise around 0:35. Individual bar attacks are not aligned.

transitions.title: Driven gestures broaden into declamation
transitions.how: The driven opening makes room for the Grandioso idea’s broad chordal statement. The change of pacing and texture enlarges the phrase, while its D-major region provides contrast to the B-minor main argument. The boundary marks the approach, not an exact Grandioso downbeat.
transitions.evidence: Grandioso at m. 105 in the formal source; audio boundary 2:24, followed by a D-major region later in the span.

transitions.title: Force is recast as a singing line
transitions.how: The sound withdraws into lyrical writing. Material associated with earlier leaping and repeated-note gestures becomes a sustained melody through altered articulation and accompaniment. The continuity is motivic rather than a literal repetition of the earlier texture.
transitions.evidence: Formal source identifies transformed themes at mm. 120 and 153; audio boundary 3:28 and pronounced quieting at 3:30–3:45.

transitions.title: Development yields to the central slow region
transitions.how: After strongly contrasted developmental writing, the tempo relaxes into the Andante sostenuto and its F♯-major region. The sustained line changes the scale of the argument without breaking the work into separate movements; familiar lyrical character survives inside the new harmonic setting.
transitions.evidence: Andante at m. 331; quieter F-sharp region near 11:00 follows the withdrawal at 10:45–10:55.

transitions.title: Quiet recollection becomes imitative movement
transitions.how: The slow region’s aftermath gives way to a fugato, initially in B♭ minor. Earlier leaping and repeated-note ideas enter a contrapuntal texture: imitation turns their contrasting identities into simultaneous activity and supplies the impetus towards the return.
transitions.evidence: Fugato m. 460 in the formal source; growing onset density and level from 17:20 through 17:45.

transitions.title: The fugato drives into the return
transitions.how: The accumulation of imitative entries leads back to the B-minor principal material. The returning argument retains the force of the opening but now follows both a slow central region and a contrapuntal transformation, so repetition functions as a return with consequences.
transitions.evidence: B-minor return m. 533; strong B-minor audio region around 18:55–19:10. Placement is approximate.

transitions.title: The largest late crest relinquishes the ending
transitions.how: The late climax stops governing the work’s scale. A sharp withdrawal makes space for a final Andante, in which opening gestures return quietly and eventually settle in B major. The final cadence is separated from the loudest point rather than reinforced by it.
transitions.evidence: Formal source: climax m. 710 and Andante m. 711; audio boundary 24:16 and fall to −32.6 dB by 24:20.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
